First off, I do agree with the general spirit of this thread that we ought to protect ordinary consumers and workers from corporate looting. I just don't think we need to rewind the modern economy to the pre-industrial age.

There might be some confusion about the term "corporation." In the law, "corporation" and "company" are the same thing. So saying we should outlaw "corporations" and instead have "responsible companies" is sort of nonsensical.

If corporations didn't exist, all businesses would have to run based on contracts. And that would get insanely complicated extremely quickly. So corporations are, in part, a way of saving resources on lawyers and paperwork.

Imagine if 20 people all wanted to invest in building a factory. Without corporations, this would have to be a complex web of contracts between all of the owners and all of their suppliers, contractors, employees, etc. As an employee, you wouldn't be employed by Factory, Inc., you would have employment contracts with all 20 owners. And what happens if they fuck you over and don't pay you? Instead of suing Factory, Inc., you have to hunt down all 20 owners for breach of contracts. It would be a mess.

Now imagine how much worse it gets in the modern economy, where thousands of people own tiny shares in a publicly traded company. The default in tort law is that a boss is responsible for all the harm his employees cause. It's called respondeat superior. If you're a 1% owner in some complex contractual arrangement of a business venture, you're on the hook for whatever harm your employees cause. If instead, you own a 1% share in a company, then the creditors can run the company into bankruptcy, but they can't suck you dry of all your assets (except in very rare situations if the company was basically just a sham).

Corporate law is pretty complicated and I'm hardly an expert in it. But there are reasons that nearly every country in the world has them! This explainer is kind of long and dense, but it has a lot of useful information: http://www.law.harvard.edu/programs/olin_center/papers/pdf/Kraakman_643.pdf
